opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that the two projects have more in common than people sometimes assume. Both are open-source, both came out of Berkeley-adjacent research communities, and both are trying to solve the same core problem: how do you serve large language models efficiently, with high throughput and low latency, on expensive hardware. There's also been a lot of healthy cross-pollination. Good ideas tend to show up in both systems eventually, and I think that's good for the whole ecosystem.

Where they differ is mostly in their origins and emphasis. vLLM's breakthrough was PagedAttention, which was really about memory management for the KV cache, treating it a bit like virtual memory in an operating system so you waste much less GPU memory and can batch more requests. That was a foundational contribution.

SGLang started from a somewhat different angle. We were looking at how people actually use LLMs in practice. It's increasingly not a single prompt and a single response. It's multi-turn chat, agents, tool calls, few-shot prompts, structured outputs, programs that call the model many times with shared context. So one of our early key ideas was RadixAttention, which automatically reuses KV cache across requests that share prefixes, organized in a radix tree. When workloads have a lot of shared structure, that reuse can give big speedups. We also put a lot of work into things like fast constrained decoding for JSON and other structured outputs, and originally a frontend language for expressing these LLM programs, hence the name, Structured Generation Language.

Over time, SGLang has also invested heavily in runtime engineering. Things like a zero-overhead CPU scheduler, so the GPU isn't sitting idle waiting on Python, and strong support for large-scale deployment: prefill-decode disaggregation, expert parallelism for big MoE models like DeepSeek, and running across many nodes. A lot of our recent energy has gone into making it work well for production at serious scale.

So if I had to summarize: vLLM has a very broad community and model coverage and has been a kind of default for many people. SGLang has tended to push hard on performance, especially for complex, structured, and agentic workloads and large-scale serving. But honestly, both teams learn from each other, and users benefit from having strong options. Competition in open source pushes everyone forward.

r001.rationale: It says the projects cross-pollinate, good ideas tend to appear in both systems, and both teams learn from each other.

r002.rationale: It describes distinct origins and emphases, then traces SGLang’s early ideas, later runtime investments, and recent production-scale focus, framing the differences over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, honestly, the first thing I'd say is that SGLang and vLLM are more similar than people sometimes assume. Both are open-source LLM serving engines, both use PagedAttention-style memory management, continuous batching, prefix caching, quantization, speculative decoding, and so on. A lot of the core ideas are shared, and the two communities have borrowed from each other quite a bit, which I think is healthy. So when people ask "which one is faster," the answer really depends on the workload and the week you measure it.

Where I think the differences come from is the starting point. vLLM began as a serving system, with PagedAttention as its key innovation, and from there it focused on being a general-purpose, very broad engine, supporting a huge range of models and hardware, and being the default that a lot of people reach for.

SGLang started from a different angle. The original motivation was about programming with LLMs, not just serving a single prompt. We were looking at agentic workloads, multi-turn chat, tree-of-thought, few-shot prompting, structured outputs, where you have a lot of shared prefixes and complex control flow between calls. So we built a frontend language for expressing those programs, and then a runtime designed around that. RadixAttention, which is our automatic KV cache reuse using a radix tree, came out of that observation that in real applications most requests overlap heavily, so you should treat cache reuse as a first-class scheduling problem rather than an afterthought. Similarly, the compressed finite state machine for constrained decoding came from wanting structured output to be fast, not just correct.

The other thing I'd point to is architecture and engineering philosophy. We've tried to keep the scheduler lean, overlap CPU scheduling with GPU execution, and do a lot of work on things like zero-overhead batch scheduling, multi-node and large-scale deployments, disaggregated prefill and decode, and expert parallelism for MoE models like DeepSeek. That's partly because many of our heaviest users run very large models at scale, so those bottlenecks became our priorities.

But I want to be fair here. vLLM has a larger community and ecosystem, and they've also done excellent work on many of these same fronts. In practice, I think the differences are less about fundamental capability and more about where each project is strongest at a given moment, and what kind of workload and team you have. For many users, both will serve them well, and the competition has really pushed the whole field forward.

r001.rationale: The response says the communities have “borrowed from each other quite a bit” and share many core ideas, describing convergence through mutual learning.

r002.rationale: It says the differences are about where each project is strongest “at a given moment,” and describes priorities shaped by their workloads and engineering focus.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame them as two systems working toward a similar goal: making large language model inference faster and more efficient, especially when you’re serving many requests at once. The difference is partly where they started and what they emphasize.

vLLM is particularly associated with efficient KV-cache management through PagedAttention. The KV cache stores intermediate attention states so the model doesn’t have to recompute them for every new token. Managing that memory efficiently helps you serve larger batches and achieve higher throughput.

SGLang puts more emphasis on the structure of the workload and the opportunities for reuse within it. For example, many requests might share a system prompt or a long document, or an application might branch into several generations from the same context. Its RadixAttention mechanism helps organize and reuse those shared prefixes, avoiding repeated computation.

But I wouldn’t draw a hard line and say one is only about memory management and the other is only about prefix caching. Both are evolving, and their capabilities overlap. For someone choosing between them, the practical question is: with your model, your hardware, and your actual traffic pattern, which gives you the latency and throughput you need? A benchmark with short, independent prompts can tell a very different story from a workload with long, shared contexts.

r001.rationale: The response says both systems are evolving and their capabilities overlap, but it does not say they learn from each other’s improvements or tend to converge.

r002.rationale: It describes their differences as starting points and emphases, then notes that both are evolving and their capabilities overlap, framing the differences as changing over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they share the same goal: making large language model inference faster and more efficient. The difference is largely in where they started and what they emphasize.

vLLM started with efficient serving, particularly memory management and batching. Its PagedAttention approach lets you manage the KV cache more efficiently, so you can serve more requests concurrently.

SGLang puts more emphasis on the structure of the application: a workload might include multiple model calls, shared prompts, branching, or structured outputs. Its runtime can take advantage of that structure. For example, RadixAttention helps reuse cached computation when requests share a prefix.

But I wouldn’t draw a rigid line between them. SGLang also serves ordinary generation requests, and vLLM also supports prefix caching and increasingly complex workloads. They’re evolving toward overlapping capabilities. For someone choosing between them, I’d look at the actual model, hardware, and traffic pattern, then compare throughput and latency under that workload. There isn’t one engine that wins in every situation.

r001.rationale: The response says the engines are evolving toward overlapping capabilities, but does not say they learn from each other’s improvements.

r002.rationale: It describes differences in where each engine started and what it emphasizes, then notes that their capabilities are evolving and overlapping.
